Article Title: 'Pee on your brain, rip your heart out': How Jensen Huang 'tortured' employees repeatedly
Article Text:
A new report details allegations of repeated humiliation, verbal abuse and threats against employees by former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

Public humiliation and threats at workplace

Complaints over management style date back to 2005

Employees divided over Huang's leadership

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang repeatedly humiliated and threatened employees during his tenure at the chipmaker, using violent language and public put-downs as part of his management style, a New York Times report said on Friday. The report, citing current and former employees, detailed incidents spanning nearly two decades, including threats to physically harm subordinates and insults directed at them during company meetings.Huang had spoken about his approach to management during a fireside chat two years ago. “I’d rather torture you into greatness because I believe in you,” he said.The accounts offer details of the management culture at Nvidia, which Huang transformed from a graphics-chip business into a major player in the artificial intelligence industry over 33 years.According to the report, Huang regularly reprimanded managers in front of their teams. In one instance, he went around a room and told managers he would kill them, a person familiar with the incident told the New York Times.When he reached an employee in their 70s, Huang reportedly said the person was very old and that everyone was hoping they would drop dead.Huang allegedly told one employee that their mother should have "aborted" them and threatened another that he would rip off their head and “pee on your brain”.In another incident, he reportedly told a subordinate he would rip both their arms off and beat them to death with them.In a separate incident, Huang allegedly threw a water bottle at an executive during a fit of anger. He also reportedly told Jay Puri, Nvidia's then-executive vice-president of worldwide field operations: “I hope you get the flu and I hope it gets worse,” and “I hope you die and put us all out of our misery.”The report traced complaints about Huang's behaviour to at least the mid-2000s. Michael Winston, a former senior vice-president of human resources, threatened legal action against Nvidia in 2005 after alleging he was fired for objecting to Huang's conduct.During a two-day off-site meeting attended by around 50 employees, Huang allegedly made violent threats. “You have to do this, or I will rip your f–king heart out and stomp on it,” he reportedly said.Winston wrote in notes at the time that Huang “thinks he can get away with anything” and that employees were “terrorized” and asking him to intervene.Winston said he confronted Huang and warned him that his behaviour had “crossed the line” and could expose the company to lawsuits. Huang allegedly described the treatment as a “rite of passage” for employees and added: “It has good entertainment value,” according to the report.Winston was fired that November. Huang reportedly told him he was “not a good fit” and threatened to ensure he would never work again if he sued the company.Winston later filed a formal complaint with California's Department of Fair Employment and Housing and drafted a lawsuit. He reached a confidential settlement with Nvidia for $1 million before the lawsuit was filed. Winston died earlier this year.Six current and former employees told the New York Times that Huang's management style had created a workplace culture they compared to Stockholm syndrome, in which hostages develop an emotional bond with their abusers.As Nvidia grew and its employees became wealthy, Huang reportedly told groups of subordinates that money alone was no longer enough to motivate them and that he needed to humiliate them.The report also said some executives adopted similar behaviour. Huang's daughter, Madison Huang, who works in marketing at Nvidia and effectively served as his de facto chief of staff, reportedly used terms such as “dead-face” for employees who remained expressionless after being reprimanded in meetings.She also allegedly called employees “goldfish” if they could not remember something, according to the Wall Street Journal.Despite the accounts of his management style, Huang retained support among many employees. More than 200,000 people have signed an online petition calling for his reinstatement as CEO.Nvidia's board has not supported the idea. Interim CEO Colette Kress, who was herself reportedly belittled by Huang during a company meeting, urged employees to “move forward” during the first all-hands meeting held without him, according to sources cited in the report.
Article Summary: Report details allegations of repeated humiliation, verbal abuse and threats against employees by former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang reportedly told one employee that their mother should have "aborted" them and threatened another that he would rip off their head and “pee on your brain”

Article Title: China bars new red-chip firms from offshore listings without shifting base
Article Text:
China's securities regulator is tightening overseas listing rules for new red-chip firms, a move that could delay IPOs and affect Hong Kong's fundraising market

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

China's securities regulator has told law firms that it will not approve overseas listing plans by red-chip companies set up after March 2023 unless they shift their domicile to mainland China, people familiar with the matter said. The move tightens Beijing's oversight of offshore fundraising and could affect Chinese companies planning to list in Hong Kong and New York.The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) conveyed the guidance to law firm representatives in recent days, the people said. They declined to be identified because the regulatory discussions were confidential, news agency Reuters reported.Red-chip companies are incorporated overseas, often in tax havens, but control businesses and assets in China through equity ownership or contractual arrangements. The structure has been popular among Chinese startups, particularly technology firms, seeking access to foreign investors and deeper capital markets.China's oversight of red-chip companies has gradually increased. Before March 2023, Chinese firms using overseas holding structures to raise funds abroad did not require regulatory approval.That changed with the introduction of new offshore listing rules in March 2023.In March this year, the CSRC told Reuters it was examining the "necessity and compliance" of red-chip structures, particularly those established after the rules came into effect.Despite the warning, some companies planning IPOs and their advisers continued to seek approval for overseas listings without dismantling their existing structures or shifting their domicile to China, one of the people said.Most failed to convince the regulator that retaining a red-chip structure was necessary, prompting the tougher stance, the person added.The move comes as China and the US compete for an edge in technology, particularly in artificial intelligence and semiconductors. Chinese authorities have stepped up scrutiny of technology, data and capital flowing outside the country.
Article Summary: China's securities regulator has told law firms that it will not approve overseas listing plans by red-chip companies set up after March 2023. The move tightens Beijing's oversight of offshore fundraising and could affect Chinese companies planning to list in Hong Kong and New York. Red- chip companies are incorporated overseas, often in tax havens, but control businesses and assets in China.

Article Title: Water, power, noise: Anthropic's first Australia data centre faces major local opposition
Article Text:
Anthropic's first Australian data centre faces strong local opposition, with 595 of nearly 600 public submissions objecting to the project or seeking a delay

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Anthropic's first data centre project in Australia has faced overwhelming opposition from local residents, with 595 of nearly 600 public submissions either objecting to the development or seeking a delay over environmental concerns. The proposed Western Downs Digital Park, located about 250 km west of Brisbane, has Anthropic as its anchor tenant and is being developed by Zerra DC, news agency Reuters reported.Only two submissions supported the project, while one was neutral, according to a filing on the proposed development. The objections largely focused on concerns over water use, electricity demand, noise, road damage from construction traffic and pressure on housing.The proposed facility is planned on farmland, away from suburban areas. However, its planned computing load of 1.44 gigawatts would make it one of Australia's biggest data centres. About one-third of the submissions came from people living within 200 km of the site, the filing said.A Zerra spokesperson said the developer took the submissions seriously, adding that they "reinforce that people want a greater say in how the project develops".The company said it was expanding its community engagement and planned to report on changes sought by the public. Anthropic declined to comment.The timeline of submissions also showed a rise in opposition after Anthropic was named as the project's tenant on September 15. The project had received five objections in a month before the announcement, while the remaining submissions came in between September 15 and November 11, when the local government stopped accepting them.The opposition comes amid growing concerns among communities about the rapid expansion of data centres, often described as AI factories, around the world. The boom in data centre infrastructure has been valued at $7 trillion by 2030 by McKinsey.
Article Summary: Anthropic's first Australian data centre faces strong local opposition. 595 of nearly 600 public submissions objecting to the project or seeking a delay. Only two submissions supported the project, while one was neutral. The proposed facility is planned on farmland, away from suburban areas.

Article Title: How Claude propelled Anthropic start-up to become a $1.76 trillion giant in 5 years
Article Text:
Anthropic Claude AI Down: Users Report Access Issues With Claude Chatbot And Claude Code

From OpenAI employees to AI industry challenger

Why investors are watching Anthropic

A first for the AI industry

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company behind chatbot Claude, has reached a valuation of roughly $1.76 trillion following its stock market debut on Nasdaq on Thursday. Founded just five years ago by former OpenAI employees, the company has made one of the fastest journeys from start-up to public listing, riding growing demand for AI technology and investor enthusiasm for the sector.The company's shares were priced at $83 each before trading began. They surged to $111.53 in the initial hours, taking its market value close to $2 trillion, before settling at $97.17 by the end of the session. The closing price represented a gain of roughly 17% over the allocation price.According to the BBC, Anthropic's listing is a crucial test for the AI industry, which has attracted enormous investment amid questions about whether the technology can justify the money being spent on it.Anthropic was founded five years ago by seven former OpenAI employees, led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei. The company has since become one of the prominent names in the AI industry, largely through its chatbot Claude.Its rise has coincided with major advances in computing power and related technology. These developments have made it possible to process far larger amounts of data and build AI chatbots that can simulate human conversations.Such tools can also perform tasks including software coding, digital image generation and internet searches. This has opened up new ways of using computers and fuelled demand for AI products.Anthropic's rapid journey from start-up to stock market listing reflects the growing interest in this technology. Its public debut also gives the company access to a wider pool of investors as it looks to finance its expansion.Anthropic's listing comes amid an unprecedented wave of spending on AI. More than $1 trillion was spent in the last year alone by a handful of major technology companies to build the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI systems.The scale of investment has raised concerns about a possible financial bubble. The industry faces several challenges, including growing competition from cheaper AI models and shortages of expensive computer chips needed to run the technology.The US Federal Reserve has also flagged concerns about high AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures. Its October meeting minutes also pointed to the concentration of AI exposure among a small number of companies.Anthropic's public listing could help it raise additional funds to meet the high costs of developing AI. Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC, "AI is financially demanding," adding that public markets open up access to more funding.As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic is entering a market where investors have few direct comparisons. Its shares could see significant fluctuations as the market assesses its prospects, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.The initial excitement around a public listing may not last, he said, pointing to the experience of Elon Musk-led SpaceX. Its shares rose about 10% on the first day of trading, taking its valuation to a record $2.2 trillion. However, they fell below their debut price within a month and have mostly declined further since.Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said: "There's no obvious peer to compare it to."Anthropic's co-founder and chief executive Dario Amodei has also been vocal about the risks posed by AI, including the possibility of a threat to human existence. The company has called for a slower pace of AI development and stronger safeguards, even as it pursues rapid growth.Reuters reported that Anthropic's market debut came as technology stocks faced pressure, with the Nasdaq Composite Index falling nearly 2.3% on Thursday. Alphabet shares dropped 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.The company's performance will now be closely watched as investors assess whether its growth prospects can justify its enormous valuation.
Article Summary: Anthropic, the company behind chatbot Claude, has reached a valuation of roughly $1.76 trillion. Founded just five years ago by former OpenAI employees, Anthropic has made one of the fastest journeys from start-up to public listing. Its listing comes amid an unprecedented wave of spending on AI.

Article Title: Anthropic's IPO: Will the record listing stop the AI bubble from bursting
Article Text:
Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, around 34% above their initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.

Can the AI boom justify its valuations?

Safety concerns and public backlash

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The next test for AI stocks

Five years after emerging as a startup founded by former OpenAI employees, Anthropic has made history with the biggest public stock offering ever. Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, around 34% above their initial public offering (IPO) price of $83, before closing at $97.17, up 17.07%.The company raised $81.31 billion through the offering, surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion fundraising haul. Its valuation briefly crossed $2 trillion during the first few minutes of trading before settling at around $1.75 trillion at the close.However, the strong debut did little to lift sentiment across the broader technology sector. US stocks came under pressure on Thursday, while Anthropic shares fell around 6% in premarket trading on Friday, slipping to $91.24.According to Reuters, the decline brought Anthropic's fully diluted valuation to around $1.7 trillion, while its market capitalisation based on shares outstanding stood at approximately $1.2 trillion.Anthropic's IPO is significant because it gives public market investors an opportunity to invest directly in an AI developer, rather than companies supplying the chips, computing infrastructure and data centres powering the technology."The reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," Fiona Cincotta from StoneX told BBC.She said previous offerings had largely involved other parts of the AI ecosystem, including semiconductor and data centre companies, while Anthropic's listing allows investors to access the AI provider itself.The offering is also expected to serve as a valuation benchmark for the wider AI industry. Its performance could influence investor sentiment towards other major players, including OpenAI, which has indicated that it could go public next year.Despite the strong demand, questions remain over whether AI companies can generate enough revenue to justify the enormous sums being invested in the technology.At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".However, the economics of the AI boom remain contentious. Companies are spending heavily on chips, data centres, computing power and talent, with some AI employees commanding annual salaries exceeding $100 million.There are also concerns about revenue concentration. Around a quarter of Anthropic's revenue reportedly comes from a handful of companies, including Google and Amazon, while the US accounts for roughly two-thirds of its revenue.The industry also has a growing network of circular financing arrangements, with companies investing in AI developers while simultaneously supplying them with chips and computing infrastructure or buying their products."Anthropic’s IPO attracted strong investor demand, with the stock opening 34% above its IPO price and closing 17% higher. However, the broader AI and technology stocks came under pressure, highlighting that a successful listing does not automatically lift the wider sector. The broader market was already under strain, and investors are reassessing valuations and the amount of capital flowing into AI," Prateek Gupta, Head of Business at Mudrex, told TOI. ""The listing also opens a new route for retail investors to access a company previously available largely through private markets. However, sustained performance will depend on business fundamentals and the ability to meet growth expectations. Investors should look beyond the initial rally and focus on valuation and long-term potential," Gupta added.Anthropic was founded by seven former OpenAI employees, including Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, over differences in their approach to AI development. The company sought to place greater emphasis on safety while building increasingly powerful AI systems.However, its rapid expansion has raised questions about whether its development pace matches its stated commitment to responsible AI.In an interview with CNBC, Amodei compared the rapid development of AI, partly driven by advanced models helping build improved versions of themselves, to allowing a driver to increase speed from 60 miles per hour to 200 miles per hour."What we've done with pacing is essentially said, 'Look, you know, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let's only drive at 90 miles an hour, spend time figuring out how to do that safely,'" he said. "And the rest of that surplus, we spend building the model in the right way."He has also warned that AI could enable biological weapons development, mass surveillance and authoritarianism, while potentially displacing millions of white-collar workers.In its filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, Anthropic devoted 93 pages to outlining potential business risks, including the possibility that advanced AI systems could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."The debate has also extended beyond the technology industry. Growing public opposition to data centres, concerns over energy and water consumption, and fears of job losses have made AI development an increasingly contentious political issue in the US.Despite these concerns, investor enthusiasm remains strong. Orders for Anthropic shares reportedly exceeded the number available by more than six times, reflecting the fear of missing out on one of the biggest technology investment opportunities.However, a strong first-day performance does not necessarily guarantee long-term gains. SpaceX shares, for instance, initially rose nearly 70% from their IPO price of $135 to $225 before falling back to around $145, according to the figures cited in the BBC report.Some investors believe Anthropic's listing could reignite enthusiasm for AI stocks."Maybe the growth of the bubble has slowed down a little bit, but actually I wouldn't be willing to say that it's about to burst yet," Eileen Burbidge, founder of tech investor Passion Capital, told BBC. "I think this IPO could actually mean everyone could be off to the races again."Cincotta, meanwhile, believes the listing could have implications far beyond Anthropic, providing a benchmark for valuations across the AI industry.
Article Summary: Anthropic shares opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17, up 17.07%. The company raised $81.31 billion through the offering, surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion fundraising haul. Its valuation briefly crossed $2 trillion during the first few minutes of trading before settling at around $1.75 trillion.

Article Title: What's next for Anthropic shares - will it boom or pop?
Article Text:
Anthropic's record-breaking IPO raises questions over the sustainability of the AI boom as costs, regulation and safety concerns loom

Revenue is soaring, but so are costs

Data centres and regulation could weigh on shares

Anthropic's safety pledge faces scrutiny

What's next for Anthropic?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Anthropic's record-breaking stock market debut has put the artificial intelligence company at the centre of a new debate over whether the AI boom can sustain its momentum. The maker of Claude chatbot ended its first day of trading on Thursday with a market valuation of around $1.75 trillion, after raising $81 billion in what was reported as the largest initial public offering ( IPO ) in history. But concerns over the industry's high spending, mounting risks and market volatility have raised questions about what lies ahead for its shares.The stock surged as much as 34% after trading began before closing about 17% above its IPO price at just over $97. The debut has made Anthropic one of the world's most valuable companies, but investors will now be watching whether the rally holds and how the company manages its growing costs, infrastructure investments and safety commitments.Why the AI market remains under pressureAnthropic's debut comes at a time when investor confidence in the broader AI industry remains unsettled. Major US stock indexes fell to seven-month lows on Thursday, while Asian markets also saw sharp declines in early trading on Friday.Despite the strong demand for Anthropic shares, analysts say its debut alone may not be enough to reassure investors about the long-term outlook for AI companies.Anthropic's rapid growth has been reflected in its revenue. According to its investor prospectus, the company generated $16.2 billion in revenue in the first six months of 2026, compared with $4.6 billion for the whole of 2025.However, the company has also reported substantial losses, including a reported $80 billion loss in the first half of 2026, largely attributed to a one-off charge. Its losses reportedly reached $104 billion in the first nine months of 2026.Anthropic is expected to spend heavily on infrastructure as it expands its AI operations. The company has plans to spend around $900 billion on data centre infrastructure over the next two decades, raising concerns about the scale of capital it may need to sustain its growth.The IPO provides the company with fresh capital for these investments, but analysts expect spending requirements and financing needs to remain a key concern for investors.Anthropic's expansion also comes amid growing opposition to AI infrastructure, particularly data centres, in the US. Protests against proposed data centre projects have gained momentum, with some municipalities and states voting for restrictions or bans.The company's growth is closely tied to investments in the infrastructure that powers AI tools such as Claude. A slowdown in data centre spending could have implications not just for Anthropic but also for the wider US economy.Regulatory scrutiny is another factor investors will be watching. Senior Democrats have signalled the possibility of tighter oversight of AI companies, citing concerns over the risks posed by advanced AI systems and the volatility that large AI IPOs could introduce into financial markets.Last month, Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, warning that the company's IPO “could inject extreme volatility and risk into the financial system, which threatens to undermine Americans' economic security.”Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, including CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, who is the company's president. The founders left OpenAI with a focus on prioritising safety in AI development.The company has repeatedly warned about the potential risks of advanced AI, even as it continues to develop increasingly powerful models. In a recent filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Anthropic devoted 93 pages to risk factors, including the possibility that advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”However, the company's safety commitments have also come under scrutiny. Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned in September, criticising the safety practices of both Anthropic and OpenAI and arguing that the industry was moving too quickly.Amodei has called for a slowdown in AI development and advocated greater coordination between companies and countries, along with independent evaluations of AI systems.Speaking at the Nasdaq opening bell on Thursday, Amodei said the company's “most difficult safety work lies ahead of us”.“And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” he said.The tension between Anthropic's safety commitments and its commercial ambitions is likely to remain a key issue as the company enters public markets.Anthropic's performance in the coming months will depend on whether it can sustain its growth while managing rising infrastructure costs, regulatory scrutiny and concerns over the risks of advanced AI. The company's expansion is also tied to data centre investments, which have faced growing opposition in the US, with some municipalities and states voting for restrictions or bans.Regulatory oversight could add another layer of uncertainty. Senior Democrats have signalled the possibility of tighter scrutiny of AI companies over the risks posed by advanced AI systems and the volatility large IPOs could introduce into financial markets.Anthropic's safety commitments are also likely to remain under scrutiny. The company has repeatedly warned about the risks of advanced AI even as it continues to develop increasingly powerful models. CEO Dario Amodei said at the Nasdaq opening bell on Thursday that the company's “most difficult safety work lies ahead of us”.The debut could also offer a signal for other AI firms planning to enter public markets. OpenAI, Anthropic's major rival, is expected to pursue an IPO in 2027. CEO Sam Altman said earlier this week that the company would go ahead with its IPO next year despite market volatility, adding, “There's been way too much investor demand and not enough supply.”
Article Summary: Anthropic's record-breaking IPO raises questions over the sustainability of the AI boom as costs, regulation and safety concerns loom. The maker of Claude chatbot ended its first day of trading on Thursday with a market valuation of around $1.75 trillion. The stock surged as much as 34% after trading began before closing about 17% above its IPO price at just over $97.

Article Title: 1.14 lakh startups generate more than 12 lakh jobs in India: Finance ministry
Article Text:
Finance Ministry

NEW DELHI: More than 1.14 lakh startups in India have created over 12 lakh jobs so far, the finance ministry said in its latest review of the Indian economy.In the report titled, ‘The Indian Economy: A Review January 2024’, the Department of Economic Affairs said that the 1.14 lakh startups recognised by the government under the 'Startup India initiative’ created more than 12 lakh jobs (as of October 2023).The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023, the document read.Despite facing global challenges in 2023 like valuation issues, few IPOs, regulatory changes and macroeconomic and geopolitical trends, India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year.The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion (from 2019 to 2023), according to a recent report by Nasscom in collaboration with Zinnov.“In 2023, despite facing global economic and regulatory challenges, Indian tech startups have prioritised the imperative of enhancing their business fundamentals, driving profitability and growth,” said Debjani Ghosh, President, Nasscom.“The proliferation of tech startups in tier 2 and 3 cities marks the ecosystem's resilience,” she added.Navigating 2024, tech startup founders expect to continue the revenue growth path with measured steps focusing on optimising expenditure and maximising profitability for B2B tech startups.Investments in deeptech will continue an upward trend in 2024. With generative AI (GenAI) acceleration, 70 per cent of start-up founders are embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in their solutions.As funding becomes scarce for the Indian startup ecosystem in general, the explosion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has given a new lease of life to entrepreneurs and founders in the country, as the Centre extends support to the sector.
Article Summary: The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023. India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year. The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion.

Article Title: Startups Revolutionizing Carbon Dioxide into Valuable Products
Article Text: For most perfume makers, ingredients to make it smell great are the most important feature. But for Stafford Sheehan, a cofounder and chemist at Air Company, the most important part of perfume-making has no scent at all.New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. While the pale yellow-color Air Eau de Parfum is about 50% more expensive than Coco Chanel’s signature No. 5, Sheehan says his product is uniquely valuable: Every 50-milliliter bottle uses 3.6 grams of CO2 that otherwise would have been released into the atmosphere. Its package reads: “Turning CO2 into something beautiful.”While the volume of CO2 utilized in the bottle is extremely small, Air Company’s perfume showcases one way the coming wave of captured carbon can be put to use. Renewable energy and electric cars alone won’t be enough to cut CO2 emissions to zero. The world will almost certainly need to capture billions of tons of the gas annually in the coming decades. Large amounts will likely be stored underground.Using it — so-called carbon capture and utilization, or CCU — to create new products from perfume to jet fuel could be an important tool in the fight against climate change, too, though the nascent industry has major hurdles to overcome.Roughly 230 million tons of CO2 are utilized every year, according to a 2019 report by the International Energy Agency. While roughly one-third of that is reused to force more oil from the ground — hardly a carbon-neutral process — CCU advocates say that the number of companies coming up with new uses for carbon has mushroomed in recent years, paving a way to unlock climate benefits. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology and lower costs.Calgary-based CleanO2 transforms CO2 captured from building heating boilers into feedstock to make soap. Newlight Technologies, a biotechnology startup based in California, takes carbon pulled directly from the air and turns it into biodegradable plastics. Germany’s Covestro AG, one of the world’s largest polymer manufacturers, is also switching some of its fossil fuel-based feedstocks to carbon-derived materials for everything ranging from car shells to medical devices and stadium roofs.Most companies working on CO2-sequestering products are still in their infancy. To grow the emerging sector, global venture capitalists in 2022 poured nearly $500 million into carbon utilization businesses, according to the IEA. That’s in stark contrast to 2015, when barely any venture money went to technologies that utilize CO2.“It’s just a whole different landscape today than it was a decade ago,” says Sasha Mackler, executive director of the energy program at Washington, DC-based non-profit Bipartisan Policy Center.Jennifer Holmgren, chief executive officer of LanzaTech Global Inc., has experienced the shifting sentiment firsthand. The Illinois-based company uses a carbon-eating bacteria – discovered in the guts of rabbits and preserved as powder – to make alternative ethanol in bioreactors not dissimilar to how breweries ferment beer. In the early 2010s, when Holmgren touted carbon-derived ethanol to prospective customers, her sales pitch was met with skepticism.But the tide began turning later that decade. In 2018, the company’s jet fuel produced from the emissions of a Chinese steel mill helped power a Transatlantic flight. LanzaTech has also inked agreements with airlines including Japan’s All Nippon Airways to supply CO2-derived jet fuel. And LanzaJet, the company’s spin-off, plans to start producing sustainable jet fuels at a commercial scale this year.Yet for all the hype around sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) using captured carbon, the industry is still an extremely small player. Almost every major airline in the world has pledged to use at least 10% sustainable jet fuels by 2030, yet SAF makes up only 0.1% of global aviation fuel supply — and much of it is made from sources other than captured CO2, such as used cooking oil.“There’s a lot more interest because consumers have become much more interested in buying things that are lower carbon,” says Holmgren. That’s enabled LanzaTech to expand the number of products that utilize CO2.American plastic container maker Plastipak, for instance, has partnered with LanzaTech to produce carbon-derived packaging materials, while polyester converted from LanzaTech’s ethanol has replaced its petroleum-based counterpart at a pilot scale in Lululemon shorts, Zara dresses, H&M yoga pants, On running shoes and Craghoppers jackets. Like SAF, though, there’s still a long way to go for CO2-derived polyester to reach meaningful levels of use.Momentum to grow beyond one-off products and low-scale production has also been supercharged by a growing array of regulations and incentives around the world. For instance, the Inflation Reduction Act that US President Joe Biden signed in 2022 raised the tax credit for carbon capture and utilization by more than 70% to $60 per metric ton in an effort to make costly projects more financially appealing.To keep the climate within habitable limits, the IEA estimates that carbon capture will have to grow to 7.6 billion tons of CO2 annually by mid-century. CCU will play a role, though just how big remains to be seen. Not every use case is created equal and some approaches, such as dissolving compressed CO2 in water to make carbonated beverages, only store the gas temporarily. To quantify the true climate benefit of carbon utilization, experts say third-party verification is badly needed.The rise of CCU technology comes as another key approach in President Biden’s net-zero roadmap is hitting a bit of a wall. Carbon capture and storage — that is, gathering CO2 as it’s released from a coal-fired power plant or other emissions source and sequestering it underground — has faced challenges because carbon is often captured in one place and stored in another. That requires pipelines to transport the gas, which many local communities have opposed. Blackrock-backed Navigator, for example, recently announced it was scrapping a planned 1,300-mile CO2 pipeline.Carbon utilization companies say that they can sidestep that issue by using carbon near or at where it’s captured.At its 12-acre factory in Brooklyn, Glenwood Mason Supply demonstrates how. The concrete manufacturer takes CO2 captured at a residential building by its partner company, CarbonQuest, and uses a technique licensed from low-carbon concrete startup CarbonCure to convert the compressed carbon into a powder not unlike dry ice. It then injects it into industrial mixers. There, the CO2 meets cement, sand and aggregate, setting off a series of chemical reactions. The final result is concrete blocks with CO2 sealed in.The technique not only stores carbon but it can also make the blocks marginally stronger. The company estimates that it has utilized about 100 tons of CO2 in total since 2020. Even if the blocks break down, the stored carbon won’t be released as CO2 because it’s been mineralized.“Cement is a big offender in carbon emissions,” says Constance Cincotta, founder of the concrete factory. She became intrigued by the technology and its ability to lower her company's climate impact after hearing about it at an industry conference in the early 2010s. But it wasn't until CarbonCure came on the scene a few years ago that the prospect of CO2-storing cement became tangible. Glenwood Mason then sourced CO2 locally from CarbonQuest, which captures carbon from buildings in New York. Those factors have enabled large-scale production.While Cincotta’s intended to help the planet, she and her team discovered that sinking CO2 into concrete blocks is good for the business, too. In 2019, New York City — where the majority of the company’s concrete blocks are sold — passed a regulation requiring all buildings to shrink their carbon footprint 40% by the end of the decade. Glenwood Mason’s phones have been ringing ever since, with calls from architects and property developers who want to leverage their lower-carbon building materials to cut emissions, says Jeff Hansen, the company’s vice president in architectural sales and marketing.The factory’s CO2-storing concrete blocks also caught the eye of Amazon.com Inc, which in 2022 persuaded a real estate developer to purchase roughly 50,000 blocks for the construction of a new warehouse in New York that Amazon has leased. Had Glenwood Mason not sealed CO2 in its blocks, it wouldn’t have won the contract, Hansen says. To figure out how to pack more carbon into its products, the company has set up a laboratory in its factory to test the reaction between CO2 and other concrete feedstocks under different temperatures and humidity levels.But figuring out the right formula is only one consideration. Utilizing CO2 often comes with an additional cost. As the demand for CO2-derived products climbs, that green premium is expected to go down. Yet “it’s very hard to be a cost parity with a 100-year-old industry that doesn’t even have to pay for its externalities,” says Holmgren of LanzaTech. Even with economies of scale, Holmgren estimates that carbon-containing fabrics will still likely cost as much as 20% higher than conventional ones.“It’s unlikely that we will ever be a cost parity,” she says.In addition to the cost barrier, CCU companies also have to convince end users that may be suspicious of unproven new technologies.Changing feedstocks “does come with risks,” says Keith Wiggins, chief executive officer of Econic Technologies, a British startup that specializes in making carbon-derived chemicals. To get risk-averse industries onboard, Wiggins says his company is laser-focused on those that are under consumer pressure to change course.That strategy seems to be working. Econic has teamed up with three manufacturers in the US, China and India to produce mattresses, outdoor garments and building insulation materials that utilize CO2. The first batch of products using the company’s technology are scheduled to enter the market in 2024.For all the promise of the carbon utilization industry, it remains to be seen if it can challenge the status quo. While Air Company started selling carbon-derived perfume in 2021, the startup has yet to build its first commercial plant, Sheehan says, citing the time-consuming process needed for collecting data and fine-tuning the technology for large-scale production.Fow now, the company’s demonstration facility in New York City — where CO2 and hydrogen gas flow through tubes into a reactor to form chemical reactions, aided by catalysts made from a confidential mixture of metals — is designed to yield at least 10,000 gallons of CO2-derived liquid annually. The limited production capacity has left many orders for its perfume — as well as jet fuels and Air Vodka, another popular product made from CO2 — unfilled.“We need to scale these facilities to the size of oil refineries today in order to have the impact on climate change that we want to have,” Sheehan says.
Article Summary: New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology.

Article Title: E-commerce firm Udaan raises $340 million ahead of planned IPO
Article Text: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain and boost vendor partnerships ahead of a stock market debut planned for 2025.The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt, the Bangalore-based company said in a statement Thursday. The round was led by M&G Plc and existing investors including Lightspeed Venture Partners and DST Global participated.The round “fully funds our business plan,” Vaibhav Gupta, Udaan co-founder and chief executive officer, said in the statement. “It enables our continued journey of growth and profitability, positioning us well to be public-market ready in the next 12-18 months.”Udaan, which competes with Reliance Industries Ltd. and Walmart Inc.’s Flipkart in helping smaller merchants source their goods, runs an online marketplace and logistics networks that help mum-and-pop stores get quicker deliveries and cut traditional middlemen out. That kind of digital-led wholesale business, though a very small part of India’s overall retail market, is expected to swell to $150 billion in sales in a decade, according to McKinsey & Co.The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas, Gupta told Bloomberg News last month.Udaan was founded in 2016 by three engineers who previously worked at Flipkart. The trio together ran the company until Gupta, one of the founders, took over as CEO in 2021. The other two founders — Amod Malviya and Sujeet Kumar — are board members.
Article Summary: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain. The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt. The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas.

Article Title: Minuscule AI startup raises $41 million to tap India growth
Article Text: A generative artificial intelligence startup targeting the Indian market raised $41 million in fresh funding, the largest such round by an early-stage AI contender in the country.Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages at price points that the country’s 1.4 billion people can afford. The Series A funding round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, and participants included Silicon Valley billionaire Vinod Khosla’s Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners, formerly Sequoia Capital India & Southeast Asia, Sarvam said Thursday.The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co-founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems as well as tools for creating apps for the meager compute infrastructure available to developers in India. The startup has a total of 18 employees and is just opening an office in the city."What we are showing is that you can build large language models with limited resources,” Raghavan said in a phone interview. "We are building at a smaller scale and demonstrating that these can be extremely cost and energy efficient so they can be accessed by everyone."Large language models, like OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama, are powerful AI systems that understand by learning from vast amounts of diverse data from the internet and elsewhere to summarize, translate, and create text, audio and video for a wide range of applications. The rivalry to develop ever-more sophisticated models is heating up in Silicon Valley and such efforts have attracted billions of dollars in investments.
Article Summary: Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages. The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co- founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems.

Article Title: ZestMoney set to shut operations this month
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Buy now Pay Later (BNPL) startup ZestMoney has decided to shut operations. The move will impact some 150 employees of the firm, the company's management told employees in a town hall on Tuesday. ZestMoney did not comment. It is learnt that the firm will shut down by the end of this month.The move comes after attempts by the Bengaluru-based startup to get acquired by larger peer PhonePe failed. The deal was called off earlier this year after a due diligence process undertaken by PhonePe, while evaluating the potential acquisition failed to meet its bar. The Walmart-owned fintech major had, however, hired some 130 of ZestMoney's employees.
Article Summary: The move will impact some 150 employees of the firm, the company's management told employees in a town hall on Tuesday. The move comes after attempts by the Bengaluru-based startup to get acquired by larger peer PhonePe failed. The Walmart-owned fintech major had, however, hired some 130 of ZestMoney's employees.

Article Title: Startups will play important role in helping India become 3rd largest economy: CEA Nageswaran
Article Text:
Chief Economic Advisor V Anantha Nageswaran

THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: Startups will play an important role in helping India become the third largest economy in the world, Chief Economic Advisor (CEA) to the Union government V Anantha Nageswaran has said.Nageswaran said that tier-2 and 3 cities, including Kerala's capital, have become game-changers in helping startups flourish in the country due to improvements in infrastructure and supportive policies of the government, according to a KSUM release.The CEA, during his Leadership Talk on the concluding day of the Huddle Global 2023 organised by the Kerala Startup Mission (KSUM), said that India was the fifth largest economy on course to become the third largest in a few years."In fact, I will say 7-in-7 is the buzz slogan, that is 7 trillion USD economy in seven years. Seven trillion USD economy size by 2030 is possible if India maintains its present growth trajectory, and in that journey startup entrepreneurs are going to play an important role," he is quoted as having said in the release.He was of the view that the active participation of startups in India in developing business models on the foundation of expanding physical and digital infrastructure will continue to generate efficiency, revenue and economic returns for the country."The last decade has seen an exceptional transformation in the startup landscape in India, which has emerged as the third largest ecosystem globally, with over 1.12 lakh startups presently recognised by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) across 763 districts."Among them, more than 110 are unicorns with a total valuation of around USD 350 billion," he said.The CEA further said that the country ranks second in innovation quality.He said that innovation in India was not just limited to certain sectors as startups were solving problems in 56 industrial sectors, with 13 per cent of them from IT services, nine per cent from health and life sciences, seven per cent from education, five per cent from agriculture and five per cent from food and beverages.Nageswaran also said it was significant that 49 per cent of the startups were from tier-2 and 3 cities which have turned to be game-changers as the business advantages in these locations enable entrepreneurs to operate at lower costs as compared to tier-1 cities."Apart from improved infrastructure and the government's pro-active policies, the availability of a technically skilled talent pool is a huge advantage for startups to set up and flourish in tier-2 and tier-3 cities," he said.He said that historically there was a perception that small towns were difficult places to conduct business."...but with improved internet penetration, vastly better physical infrastructure, road, rail and air connectivity and
